title: Energizing the Team That Faces Repetitive Tasks and Travel
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses the morale cost of repetitive work and travel, quoting NBA coach Pat Riley on how fatigue and monotony, not talent or effort, cause teams to 'go sideways' over a long season. The author rejects the idea that this kind of burnout is simply an inevitable cost of repetitive roles, arguing instead that leaders can actively counter it by injecting variety into the sameness. Concretely, the piece suggests scheduling a new activity during repeat travel, and applies the same principle to repetitive projects by rotating in new colleagues or new processes.
points: Fatigue and monotony, not lack of talent or effort, are what cause teams to 'go sideways' over long stretches of repetitive work.
The piece rejects treating burnout from repetition as inevitable, arguing leaders can actively counter it by deliberately varying the routine.
Concrete tactics offered include scheduling new activities during repeat travel and rotating new colleagues into repetitive projects.
The central reframe: monotony isn't intrinsic to a repeated task itself, but to doing it with the same approach, thinking, and people.
quotes: Leaders and team members who are repetitively tasked with the same assignments, travel, and engagements often lose energy and enthusiasm for the work over time.

Players have a tendency to go sideways on you, not for any other reason than fatigue, boredom, monotony. Eighty-two games, 30 cities, same place, same arenas, same locker rooms, same hotels, same food.
Great leaders don’t accept the idea that monotony and fatigue are inevitable and must simply be endured.
Doing the same task or assignment is only monotonous if it is done with the same approach, with the same thinking, and with the same people.
The cure for boredom is curiosity and great leaders encourage it, sometimes to the point of insisting on it.
